solid.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
solid.simpleExplanation:
*"A class should have one, and only one, reason to change."*  
It does **not** mean "a class can only have 1 method." It means all methods in a class belong to **one cohesive job** (serving one stakeholder/actor).
solid.whyItExists: If `Invoice` calculates taxes, prints PDFs, AND emails customers, then changing the email SMTP library risks breaking tax calculation! Separating concerns keeps bugs isolated and makes unit testing effortless.
solid.whatsWrong: Three unrelated responsibilities live inside `Invoice`. Every formatting change or database/file migration forces editing and recompiling `Invoice`.
solid.improvementExplanation: `Invoice` handles only financial logic; `InvoicePrinter` handles presentation; `InvoiceRepository` handles persistence. Each can evolve and be tested independently.
solid.analogy: In a restaurant, the **Chef** cooks, the **Waiter** serves, and the **Accountant** handles billing. If the Chef also mopped tables and processed credit cards, food quality and speed would collapse.
solid.violations:
- God classes (`Manager`, `System`, `Utils`) with 20 unrelated methods.
- Domain entities containing `std::cout`, SQL strings, or HTTP calls.

questions.question: Does SRP mean every class should have only one function?
questions.answer: No—`Stack` has `push`, `pop`, `top`, `empty`, all serving one responsibility: LIFO storage.

questions.question: What is the risk of over-applying SRP ("class explosion")?
questions.answer: Splitting tiny 3-line helpers into dozens of artificial classes hurts readability. Split along **independent reasons to change** (actors).

questions.question: How does SRP help unit testing?
questions.answer: You can test `Invoice::calculateTotalWithTax()` without spinning up a printer or filesystem.

questions.question: If `User` validates passwords AND hashes them with SHA-256, does that violate SRP?
questions.answer: Yes if hashing algorithms change separately—extract `IPasswordHasher`.

questions.question: How does SRP interact with the Rule of 0?
questions.answer: Rule of 0 embodies SRP: memory/resource management lives in `std::unique_ptr`/`std::vector`, leaving domain classes focused on business logic!

practiceProblems.title: Design a `Book` module:
practiceProblems.prompt: Separate book metadata (`Book`), borrowing rules (`LibraryPolicy`), and JSON serialization (`BookSerializer`) so changing JSON library doesn't touch `Book`.
practiceProblems.solution: `Book` holds `isbn/title/author`; `BookSerializer` reads `const Book&` and emits JSON string; `LibraryPolicy` enforces loan limits.

solid.title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
solid.simpleExplanation:
*"Software entities should be **open for extension**, but **closed for modification**."*  
You should be able to add a new feature (like a new discount or payment type) by adding a **new class**, without modifying already-tested existing code.
solid.whyItExists: Every time you edit a working function to add an `else if` branch, you risk introducing regressions into existing cases and forcing re-testing of the entire module.
solid.whatsWrong: Adding a 3rd, 4th, or 10th discount forces editing `DiscountCalculator::apply()` repeatedly.
solid.improvementExplanation: Adding `StudentDiscount` requires zero edits to `Checkout` or existing discounts—just write one new subclass!
solid.analogy: A **USB port** on a laptop: you can plug in a mouse, keyboard, SSD, or webcam (open for extension) without cracking open the laptop motherboard and soldering wires (closed for modification).

questions.question: Does OCP mean you can NEVER edit existing code, even for bug fixes?
questions.answer: No! Bug fixes and requirement changes to existing behavior still edit code; OCP aims to prevent editing stable orchestration code when *extending* variations.

questions.question: How do C++ templates achieve OCP without `virtual` functions?
questions.answer: Compile-time polymorphism (e.g., `std::sort` accepts any comparator lambda/functor without modifying `std::sort`!).

questions.question: Where does the `if/else` or `switch` eventually move when you apply OCP?
questions.answer: To a single composition root / Factory (`CompressorFactory`) at the boundary of the app!

questions.question: How do Strategy and Decorator patterns enforce OCP?
questions.answer: Strategy extends algorithms via new policy classes; Decorator wraps new behaviors around existing interfaces without modifying them.

questions.question: Can inheritance violate OCP if overused?
questions.answer: Yes, if base classes expose fragile protected state that breaks when subclasses extend them—prefer clean pure interfaces.

solid.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
solid.simpleExplanation: *"Objects of a `Derived` class should be usable everywhere a `Base` class is expected, without breaking program correctness or surprising the caller."*
solid.whyItExists: Runtime polymorphism collapses if callers have to write `if (type == Penguin) don't call fly();`—because `Derived` broke the behavioral promise made by `Base`.
solid.whatsWrong: `Rectangle` promises `setHeight` leaves `width` unchanged. `Square` breaks that postcondition!
solid.improvementExplanation: Both `Rectangle` and `Square` honor `IShape::area()` cleanly with no conflicting mutable setter contracts.
solid.analogy: If a recipe asks for a **Payment Card** that supports `swipe()`, handing it a **Gift Voucher** that crashes on `swipe()` breaks substitution—even though both "pay for things."
solid.violations:
- Overridden methods that `throw std::logic_error("Not implemented")`.
- Empty no-op overrides (`void fly() override {}` on `Ostrich : Bird`).
- Strengthening preconditions (Base accepts any `int >= 0`; Derived rejects `int > 100`).

questions.question: What are the precondition and postcondition rules of LSP?
questions.answer: Derived cannot require **more** (stronger preconditions) than Base, and cannot promise **less** (weaker postconditions) than Base.

questions.question: How do you model `Bird`, `Eagle`, and `Penguin` without violating LSP?
questions.answer: Keep `Bird` focused on shared traits (`eat()`), and put `fly()` in a separate `IFlyable` interface implemented only by `Eagle`!

questions.question: Does `ReadOnlyFile : public File` (where `write()` throws) violate LSP?
questions.answer: Yes! Split into `IReadable` and `IWritable` (LSP + ISP together).

questions.question: How do Covariant Return Types satisfy LSP?
questions.answer: If `Base::clone()` promises "returns a `Base*`", `Derived::clone()` returning `Derived*` fulfills a *stronger* guarantee (`Derived*` is-a `Base*`), completely safe for callers!

questions.question: Can private/protected inheritance violate LSP?
questions.answer: No—LSP applies to **public inheritance** ("is-a" substitutability); private inheritance hides the base conversion completely.

### LSP Practice Problems (2)
1. **Fix `Bird` Hierarchy:** Refactor `Bird { fly(), swim() }` with `Sparrow` and `Penguin` so no class stubs/throws `fly()`.
practiceProblems.solution: `Bird { eat() }`, `IFlyable { fly() }`, `ISwimmable { swim() }`; `Sparrow : Bird, IFlyable`; `Penguin : Bird, ISwimmable`.

practiceProblems.title: Fix `Account` Withdrawals:
practiceProblems.prompt: Refactor `Account { withdraw() }` + `FixedDepositAccount` (cannot withdraw early!) without throwing in `withdraw()`.
practiceProblems.solution: Base `Account { deposit(), balance() }`, subclass `WithdrawableAccount : Account { virtual bool withdraw() }`; `FixedDepositAccount : Account` has `withdrawOnMaturity()`.

solid.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
solid.simpleExplanation:
*"Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces (methods) they do not use."*  
Prefer several small, specific interfaces over one giant "all-in-one" interface.
solid.whyItExists: When a fat interface changes one unrelated method, every implementing class—even ones that never used that method—must recompile and deal with dummy overrides.
solid.whatsWrong: `OldPrinter` only prints, yet `IMachine` forces it to implement `scan()` and `fax()`, causing LSP breakage too!
solid.improvementExplanation: In C++, multiple inheritance of pure interfaces is completely safe and zero-diamond-state! Each device implements *only* what it truly supports.
solid.analogy: A restaurant **menu** divided into Vegetarian, Vegan, and Drinks sections—rather than forcing every customer to order a mandatory combo containing meat, dairy, and coffee!
solid.violations:
- Interfaces with 10+ unrelated methods (`IUserManager` doing auth + billing + email + analytics).
- Implementing classes throwing `NotImplemented` on half the interface.

questions.question: How does ISP differ from SRP?
questions.answer: SRP guides how big a *concrete class's* responsibilities should be; ISP guides how narrow a *client-facing abstract interface* should be.

questions.question: How does C++ implement ISP cleanly compared to single-inheritance concerns?
questions.answer: C++ supports inheriting multiple stateless abstract classes (`public IPrinter, public IScanner`) directly.

questions.question: Can an interface have ONLY 1 pure virtual method (Single-Method Interface)?
questions.answer: Yes! (e.g., `IRunnable`, `IComparator`, `ISerializable`—very idiomatic!)

questions.question: How do ISP and LSP reinforce each other?
questions.answer: Splitting fat interfaces removes forced dummy methods, eliminating the main source of LSP violations!

questions.question: Can a class implement two separate interfaces that have the exact same method signature `void reset()`?
questions.answer: Yes—in C++, a single `void reset() override` satisfies both, *unless* they mean completely different things (then intermediate wrapper classes disambiguate).

solid.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
solid.simpleExplanation: *"High-level modules (business rules) should NOT depend on low-level modules (MySQL, file system, SMTP). Both should depend on **abstractions** (interfaces)."*
solid.whyItExists: If `OrderProcessor` directly instantiates `MySQLDatabase`, switching to PostgreSQL—or testing `OrderProcessor` without a live database—forces rewriting `OrderProcessor`.
solid.whatsWrong: `OrderService` (high-level) hardcodes `ConsoleEmailSender` (low-level). You cannot swap in SMS or a mock during unit tests!
solid.improvementExplanation: The dependency arrow is *inverted*: `EmailNotifier` depends on `INotifier`, and `OrderService` also depends on `INotifier`. Unit tests can pass a `MockNotifier` in 1 microsecond!
solid.analogy: A **wall power socket** (abstraction): your lamp doesn't solder directly into the coal power plant's turbine; both the house wiring and the lamp depend on the standard 3-pin socket interface!
solid.violations:
- Calling `new ConcreteService()` or holding `MySQLClient db_;` directly inside high-level business classes.
- Calling global singletons (`Database::getInstance().query(...)`) inside domain logic.

questions.question: What is the difference between Dependency Inversion (DIP) and Dependency Injection (DI)?
questions.answer: **DIP** is the *architectural principle* (depend on abstractions). **DI** is the *technique* of passing dependencies from outside (constructor/setter/parameter injection) instead of `new`ing them inside.

questions.question: Who owns the interface in DIP—the high-level module or the low-level module?
questions.answer: The **high-level module** defines what interface it needs (`INotifier`), and the low-level module implements it!

questions.question: Compare Constructor Injection vs Setter Injection.
questions.answer: Constructor injection guarantees required dependencies are non-null and immutable from birth; setter injection allows optional/swappable dependencies later.

questions.question: How does C++ achieve DIP with zero `virtual` overhead using templates?
questions.answer: `template <typename Notifier> class OrderService { Notifier& n_; };`—compile-time policy injection!

questions.question: What is a Composition Root?
questions.answer: The single place at program startup (`main()`) where concrete objects are instantiated and wired into high-level services.
